objectives: Share and take turns during play

explanation: When two friends want the same toy, they can take turns: first one friend plays, then the other. Saying "my turn, your turn" helps.

lessons.title: The Magic Words
objectives: Use please, thank you, sorry and excuse me
Say sorry and help make things better
explanation: Some words are like magic because they make people feel respected: please (when asking), thank you (when someone helps), sorry (when we hurt someone) and excuse me (to get past or interrupt).
Kind words make people smile. Hurtful words, like calling names, make people sad — even if we didn't mean it.
When we make a mistake, we say sorry and try to fix it: helping rebuild a tower we knocked over, or getting a tissue for a friend who is crying.

lessons.title: Can I Play Too?
objectives: Use friendly ways to join a game
Invite someone who is alone to play
explanation: Making friends starts with small steps: smile, say hello and your name, and ask a question: "What are you building?"
To join a game, watch for a moment, then ask: "Can I play too?" If they say not now, that's okay — try another game or ask later.
Good friends also notice others who are alone and invite them: "Do you want to play with us?" That can make someone's whole day.

lessons.title: Talk It Out
objectives: Use I-statements to express a problem
Find a fair solution with someone
explanation: Disagreements happen between friends — that's normal. What matters is solving them without hurting each other.
Steps: cool down first. Then use an I-statement: "I feel upset when you take my ball without asking. I'd like you to ask first." Listen to the other person's side too.
Together, think of solutions and choose one that is fair for both — a win-win. If you're stuck, ask an adult to help.

lessons.title: Everyone Belongs Here
objectives: Describe ways people are different and the same
Include others regardless of differences
explanation: People are different in many ways: families (big, small, one parent, grandparents), languages, religions, food, skin colour, abilities and interests. These differences make our world rich.
We are also the same in important ways: everyone wants to feel safe, loved and included.
A stereotype is an unfair idea that everyone in a group is the same, like "boys don't dance" or "girls aren't good at sports". Stereotypes are wrong and can hurt. Everyone deserves to be included.

lessons.title: What Is Bullying?
objectives: Define bullying and distinguish it from ordinary conflict
Describe types and effects of bullying
explanation: Bullying is when someone deliberately and repeatedly hurts another person who finds it hard to defend themselves. A single argument between equals is a conflict, not bullying — though it still needs sorting out.

Bullying can be physical (hitting, pushing), verbal (name-calling, threats), social (leaving someone out on purpose, spreading rumours) or online (cyberbullying: mean messages, sharing embarrassing photos).
Bullying can make people feel scared, sad, lonely and anxious. It is never the target's fault, and it should always be reported to a trusted adult.

vocabulary.meaning: repeated, deliberate hurting of someone who finds it hard to defend themselves

examples: Being left out of every group on purpose, day after day — social bullying.

story.title: Not Just Teasing
story.text: Every day, a group called Meena names because of her glasses and hid her tiffin. "It's just a joke," they said. But Meena dreaded school. When she finally told her teacher, the teacher explained that repeated, deliberate hurt is bullying — and it would stop. It did, with help from the school.

lessons.title: From Bystander to Upstander
objectives: Explain the role of bystanders
Choose safe upstander actions
explanation: A bystander sees bullying but doesn't help. An upstander takes action to help — safely.
Upstander actions: don't laugh or join in; say "Stop, that's not okay" if it's safe; help the target get away; be friendly to them afterwards; and tell a trusted adult.
You don't have to be a hero or fight. Even small actions — sitting with someone who was left out — can change how they feel. Research shows bullying often stops quickly when peers step in.

vocabulary.meaning: someone who sees something happen but doesn't act

lessons.title: Green Flags and Red Flags
objectives: Identify healthy and unhealthy relationship behaviours
Know how to respond to unhealthy patterns
explanation: Healthy friendships have "green flags": respect for each other's choices, trust, honesty, support, fun, and freedom to have other friends.
"Red flags" include controlling behaviour (telling you who you can talk to), constant put-downs, pressure to do things you don't want to, jealousy that limits you, and threats.
Friendships change as we grow; sometimes we drift apart, and that's okay. If a relationship feels controlling or harmful, talk to a trusted adult. You deserve respect.

lessons.title: Passive, Aggressive or Assertive?
objectives: Distinguish passive, aggressive and assertive communication
Respond assertively to peer pressure
explanation: Passive communication means not expressing your needs — going along to avoid conflict. Aggressive communication means expressing needs in a way that hurts or disrespects others.
Assertive communication is the healthy middle: clearly and calmly expressing your feelings and needs while respecting others. "I don't want to skip class. I'll see you at lunch."
Assertive body language: steady voice, eye contact, calm posture. Online, the same rules apply — pause before posting and avoid group pile-ons.

vocabulary.meaning: not standing up for your needs

examples: Passive: "Umm, okay, I guess I'll do it." Aggressive: "You're an idiot for asking!" Assertive: "No thanks, that's not for me."

units.title: The Psychology of Groups
units.summary: Why groups influence us so strongly.
objectives: Explain conformity and in-group bias

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Why We Go Along
objectives: Explain conformity and in-group bias
Evaluate how group pressure affects decisions
explanation: In the 1950s, Solomon Asch asked people to judge which of several lines matched a reference line. When actors in the group deliberately chose the wrong answer, many real participants went along at least some of the time — showing the power of conformity.
People tend to favour their own group (in-group) and judge outsiders (out-group) more harshly, even when groups are formed randomly. This can fuel prejudice.
Groupthink happens when a group values agreement over good decisions, silencing doubts. Encouraging dissent, a "devil's advocate", and diverse members helps groups decide better.

context.text: Later researchers have discussed how culture and context influence conformity rates; Asch also found that a single dissenter greatly reduced conformity.

vocabulary.meaning: changing behaviour to match a group
a group you belong to
poor decisions from valuing agreement over critical thinking
disagreement with the majority

examples: Laughing at a joke you don't find funny because everyone else is.
A team ignoring warning signs to avoid conflict.

story.title: One Voice Is Enough
story.text: In Asch's experiments, when just one other person in the room gave the correct answer, participants were far more likely to trust their own eyes. A single dissenting voice broke the spell. Sometimes being that one voice helps others speak up too.

activities.prompt: In Asch's studies, conformity dropped when…
options: one other person disagreed with the group

activities.prompt: Groups can make poor decisions when doubts are silenced.

thinking: When is conformity helpful? When is it harmful?
How can you encourage dissent in a friendly way?
speaking: Lead a decision-making discussion where you deliberately invite a devil's advocate.

lessons.title: Building Belonging
objectives: Explain why belonging matters for wellbeing
Design an initiative that builds inclusion
explanation: Belonging — feeling accepted and valued — is a basic human need. Research links strong social connection to better mental and physical health.
People hold many identities: family, region, language, religion, interests. Healthy communities make room for multiple identities rather than forcing everyone to be the same.

Service strengthens communities. Many traditions value service: seva in Sikhism and Hinduism, sadaqah in Islam, dana in Buddhism, and volunteering in secular life. Inclusive initiatives — buddy systems, clubs for all, accessible events — help everyone belong.

context.text: Many religious traditions teach service to others as a spiritual practice, such as seva (selfless service) in Sikhism, expressed in community kitchens (langar).

vocabulary.meaning: feeling accepted and valued in a group
who you are and the groups you feel part of
selfless service
networks of relationships that help a community work

examples: A school buddy system for new students.
Neighbours organising a clean-up and shared meal.

story.title: The Buddy Bench
story.text: A student noticed that new and quiet students often ate alone. She proposed a "buddy bench": anyone sitting there was saying, "I'd like company." Students took turns checking the bench. Within months, the school's survey showed more students felt they belonged.

activities.prompt: People can hold many identities at once.

options: a buddy system for new students
a club with a secret invite list

thinking: What makes you feel you belong somewhere?
How can a community welcome newcomers while keeping its traditions?
speaking: Pitch an inclusion initiative to your school or residential society.

project.safety: Ask permission before surveying peers, make participation voluntary and anonymous, and avoid sensitive questions. Work with a trusted adult and report only group-level results.
